rw: A quality standard is a measure or rule a product must meet to be acceptable, such as size, strength or safety limits, so products are consistent and customers know what to expect.

ww.A slogan that the company uses in its ad: A slogan is a catchy advertising phrase used to promote a brand, not a measure of how good a product must be.
ww.A discount offered to loyal customers of: A loyalty discount is a pricing and promotion tool that rewards repeat buyers; it says nothing about the level of quality a product must reach.
ww.A schedule for delivering products to th: A delivery schedule is a logistics and operations plan for when goods arrive; it does not define the level of quality a product must meet.

rw: ISO 9001 is an international standard from the International Organization for Standardization that sets requirements for quality management systems, helping firms show they consistently meet customer needs and improve their processes.

ww.A tax form for international sales, file: A customs form for international sales is a trade document; ISO 9001 is not a tax form and has nothing to do with filing duties.
ww.A law that sets minimum wages for worker: Minimum wage rules come from government labor law such as the Fair Labor Standards Act; ISO 9001 is a voluntary standard, not a wage law.
ww.A union agreement for workers about pay: Union agreements covering pay and hours are called collective bargaining contracts; ISO 9001 is not a labor agreement but a quality management standard.

rw: Certification, checked by an outside auditor, shows customers a supplier's processes meet a recognized quality standard, which builds trust, helps win contracts and often is required by large buyers.

ww.To avoid inspecting its own products eve: Certification does not end inspections; ISO 9001 requires ongoing checks, records and audits, so a certified supplier still must verify its own products.
ww.To raise the price of its goods above co: ISO 9001 does not set or raise prices; certification may help win business, but price depends on costs and competition rather than the standard itself.
ww.To stop customers from comparing supplie: Customers can always compare suppliers on price and quality; certification gives buyers more information about quality, it does not stop them from comparing.

rw: Six Sigma is a data-driven method that aims to cut defects and variation in processes, targeting about 3.4 defects per million opportunities, using steps like DMAIC to improve quality.

ww.A method of setting six different prices: Six Sigma is about process quality, not pricing; setting several prices for one product would be price discrimination or tiered pricing, an unrelated idea.
ww.A method of printing six copies of repor: Printing copies of reports is a clerical task; Six Sigma is a quality improvement method and has nothing to do with producing six report copies.
ww.A method of hiring six new managers for: Six Sigma does not mean hiring six managers; the name comes from a statistical measure of variation, and the method focuses on defects, not staffing.

rw: Benchmarking compares a firm's performance, products or processes against the best in the industry to find gaps and learn practices that can raise its own quality and efficiency.

ww.Ignoring rivals to focus on a firm's own: Benchmarking looks outward at other firms; ignoring rivals to use only internal data is the opposite of comparing against the best performers.
ww.Setting the lowest possible goals for a: Benchmarking is used to find higher targets and improve; setting the lowest possible goals would prevent improvement rather than measure against the best.
ww.Counting the benches in a company's fron: Benchmarking has nothing to do with literal benches; it is a management comparison technique, and counting lobby furniture measures no performance at all.

rw: Comparing the firm's on-time rate with the industry leader's is benchmarking, a quality technique that measures performance against the best so the company can see gaps and set improvement goals.

ww.Market study: A market study researches customers, demand and competitors to guide decisions; it does not compare on-time delivery performance against an industry leader.
ww.Price fixing: Price fixing is an illegal agreement among competitors to set prices; comparing delivery performance with a leader is unrelated to it.
ww.Stock counting: Stock counting is an inventory task that tallies goods on hand; it does not measure delivery performance against a competitor.

rw: A customer complaint is a statement that a product or service did not meet expectations, which gives a firm direct feedback it can use to find and fix quality problems.

ww.A compliment about excellent service fro: A compliment praises good service; a complaint is the opposite, since it reports that something fell short of what the customer expected.
ww.An order for more products from a custom: An order for more products is a sale; it shows demand but does not report dissatisfaction, so it is not a complaint.
ww.A request to open a new account at a ban: Asking to open an account is a banking service request; it expresses no dissatisfaction, so it is not a complaint.

rw: Complaints are valuable feedback that can reveal quality problems, so firms should record, respond and use them to improve products and service, which also helps win back unhappy customers.

ww.Blame the customer for every issue that: Blaming customers hides real problems and drives them away; effective firms listen to complaints instead of pointing fingers at buyers.
ww.Ignore them so staff stay positive and a: Ignoring complaints may feel comfortable but leaves problems unsolved, loses customers and invites bad word of mouth, which harms the business more than hearing the bad news.
ww.Delete them from the record to keep the: Deleting complaints erases the evidence needed to spot patterns and fix causes; tidy files are not worth losing information about quality.

rw: A root cause is the underlying reason a problem happens; fixing it prevents the problem from returning, while fixing only symptoms leaves the cause in place.

ww.The cost of fixing the problem once: The cost of fixing a problem measures its impact after the fact; it does not tell you why the problem happens, which is the root cause.
ww.The first person who noticed the problem: Who first noticed a problem is just a reporting detail; the root cause is the underlying reason, not the person who spotted it.
ww.The most visible symptom of the problem: The most visible symptom is the surface effect of a problem; fixing only symptoms lets the real cause keep producing the same trouble.

rw: Finding and fixing the root cause, such as poor packing or rough handling, stops the damage at its source, saves replacement costs and keeps customers satisfied.

ww.Keep replacing items forever without che: Replacing items forever treats the symptom, costs money each time and never prevents damage; the shipments will keep breaking without a look at why.
ww.Blame customers for the damage done to t: Blaming customers does not explain damage that occurs in transit, and it hurts the store's reputation without stopping the damage itself.
ww.Stop selling any products that come in b: Stopping sales of everything that ships is an extreme overreaction that loses revenue and still leaves the actual packing or handling problem unsolved.

rw: A quality audit is a systematic review that checks whether quality procedures and standards are followed, finding gaps so the firm can correct them before customers are affected.

ww.A review of employees' vacation days and: Reviewing vacation requests is an HR and payroll task; a quality audit looks at procedures and products, not employee time off.
ww.A review of competitors' prices and adve: Reviewing competitors' prices and advertising is market analysis; a quality audit examines the firm's own procedures, not rivals' marketing.
ww.A review of how much tax a firm owes, do: Checking how much tax a firm owes is a tax audit by a tax agency; a quality audit reviews quality procedures instead.

rw: Warranty claims are made when products fail or disappoint, so a rise in claims is a sign of a possible quality problem in design, materials or manufacturing.

ww.A growing market for a new product line: A growing market shows up as rising sales and demand; warranty claims arise when products fail, so they signal problems instead of growth.
ww.A successful promotion campaign last mon: A successful promotion would raise sales or awareness; warranty claims come after purchase from product failures, not from advertising effectiveness.
ww.A fall in the product's price last month: A price drop affects what customers pay; warranty claims are tied to product performance after the sale, not to the price charged.

rw: A 40 percent jump in claims signals a likely defect, so management should investigate the cause and take corrective action to protect customers, costs and the brand.

ww.Remove all warranties from the product l: Removing warranties would not fix the defect; it would anger customers, hurt trust and probably cut sales while the product still fails.
ww.Ignore the rise because sales are up ove: Rising sales do not excuse a sharp rise in claims; ignoring it lets a defect spread to more customers and increases repair costs.
ww.Raise the price of the model immediately: Raising the price by half does not address why the model fails and would likely hurt sales while the quality problem continues.

rw: A service quality gap is the difference between what customers expect and what they actually receive; closing it improves satisfaction and loyalty.

ww.The difference between a firm's sales an: The difference between sales and yearly goals is a performance gap against targets; it is not about customers' expectations versus service received.
ww.The difference between a firm's cost and: The difference between cost and sale price is the profit margin; it is a financial measure, not a service quality gap.
ww.The difference between two competing pro: A difference between competitors' prices is a price gap in the market; it says nothing about how service compares to customer expectations.

rw: The hotel promised quiet rooms but guests experience noise, so what customers expect differs from what they get, which is a service quality gap that harms satisfaction and reviews.

ww.A pricing strategy: Pricing strategy is about setting what customers pay; a noisy hallway is a failure to deliver a promised service quality, not a price decision.
ww.A channel decision: A channel decision is about distribution, how products reach customers; noisy hallways are a service experience problem instead.
ww.A successful promotion: A successful promotion would attract guests; here the hotel's promise did not match reality, which damages satisfaction rather than showing promotion success.

rw: Zero defects is a goal of striving to do every task and product right the first time, preventing errors instead of fixing them later, which reduces waste and rework.

ww.Producing nothing so no defects can ever: Zero defects does not mean producing nothing; it means making products correctly, so idle production would make no sense as a quality goal.
ww.Hiding defects from customers who buy th: Hiding defects from customers is deceptive and unethical, and it may be illegal; zero defects aims to prevent defects, not conceal them.
ww.Accepting any number of defects as quite: Accepting any number of defects is the opposite of zero defects, which sets perfection as the goal even if it is hard to reach.

rw: Just-in-time makes goods only as they are needed, with materials arriving as production requires, which cuts storage costs, waste and tied-up cash.

ww.Making large amounts of goods far ahead: Making large amounts far ahead of orders is mass production for stock, which builds inventory; JIT does the opposite by matching output to demand.
ww.Making goods only once each year in a si: Producing once a year in a single batch creates huge inventory and long waits; JIT produces frequently in small amounts as needed.
ww.Making goods without any plan for what i: JIT depends on careful planning and close coordination with suppliers; producing without any plan would cause shortages or waste, not efficiency.

rw: Because JIT holds little stock, a supply delay can halt production, and that makes dependable suppliers critical to avoid costly shutdowns and late orders.

ww.Paying high storage costs for huge stock: High storage costs for huge stockpiles are a problem of traditional stock-heavy methods; JIT reduces that cost instead of creating it.
ww.Having too much unsold inventory in stor: Too much unsold inventory is what JIT is meant to avoid, since it produces only what is needed, so this is not its risk.
ww.Wasting materials through overproduction: Overproduction of unwanted goods is the waste JIT targets by producing to order, so it is a benefit of JIT rather than a risk.

rw: Customer satisfaction is how well a product or service meets or exceeds expectations, and satisfied customers tend to return, buy more and recommend the business.

ww.The number of products a company makes e: Daily output counts production volume; it measures what a plant makes, not how customers feel about what they received.
ww.The number of stores a company owns in t: The number of stores measures company size and reach, not whether customers are happy with products or service.
ww.The price a customer pays for a product: The price paid is a cost to the customer; satisfaction depends on how value and quality compare to expectations, not on price alone.

rw: Listening to feedback and fixing recurring problems shows customers they are valued and removes the causes of dissatisfaction, which raises satisfaction and loyalty over time.

ww.Making returns more difficult for the cu: Making returns harder frustrates buyers and lowers trust; easy returns usually raise satisfaction, so this choice would reduce it.
ww.Reducing the training that service staff: Cutting training leaves staff less able to help, which leads to more mistakes and unhappy customers, so satisfaction would fall.
ww.Ignoring feedback to save time and effor: Ignoring feedback saves little time and lets problems continue, so customers stay unhappy and may leave for competitors.

rw: Risk is the chance that something will cause loss or harm, such as theft, injury, fire or lawsuits, and managing it helps businesses protect people, assets and profits.

ww.A reward for taking a good decision at w: A reward is a positive result of a good decision; risk concerns the possibility of loss or harm, not a payoff.
ww.A certain outcome that cannot be avoided: Risk involves uncertainty; a certain outcome that no one can avoid is not a risk but a known event.
ww.A report on past results of the firm for: A report on past results is a record of what already happened; risk looks ahead at the possibility of loss.

rw: Risk management means identifying, assessing and reducing risks, using steps like avoiding, reducing, transferring or accepting them to protect people, property and profits.

ww.Ignoring risks until a loss occurs at wo: Ignoring risks until a loss occurs is reactive and costly; risk management is planned and proactive, aiming to prevent losses before they happen.
ww.Taking as many risks as you possibly can: Taking as many risks as possible would invite losses; risk management weighs risks and controls them, not seeks them out.
ww.Avoiding all customers in the market: Avoiding all customers would end the business; risk management targets specific threats and does not mean giving up on sales.

rw: The four basic ways to handle risk are to avoid, reduce, transfer or accept it, and a firm picks the one that fits how likely and costly the risk is.

ww.Ignore, hide, delay or deny the risk: Ignoring, hiding, delaying or denying risks are poor habits, not recognized strategies; none of them actually reduces the chance or impact of a loss.
ww.Buy, sell, trade or lend the risk: Buying, selling, trading or lending are financial or commercial actions; they are not the standard strategies for handling a risk.
ww.Print, store, mail or recycle it: Printing, storing, mailing or recycling are paperwork or waste tasks, not risk management strategies recognized in business.

rw: Risk avoidance means choosing not to do an activity that carries a risk, such as declining to sell a dangerous product, which removes the chance of loss completely.

ww.Accepting the risk and planning to cover: Accepting the risk and planning for losses is risk acceptance, where the firm chooses to bear the loss instead of avoiding it.
ww.Buying insurance to cover a loss that ma: Buying insurance is risk transfer, because it shifts the financial burden of a possible loss to an insurer instead of avoiding the activity.
ww.Taking steps to lower the chance of a lo: Taking steps to lower the chance of a loss is risk reduction, such as safety training, while avoidance removes the activity entirely.

rw: Risk transfer shifts the financial burden of a risk to another party, most often through insurance or contracts, so the firm is protected if a loss happens.

ww.Lowering the chance of the loss with saf: Lowering the chance of loss with safety steps and training is risk reduction, which keeps the risk but makes it smaller.
ww.Avoiding the activity altogether to remo: Avoiding the activity altogether is risk avoidance, which removes the risk rather than moving the financial burden to someone else.
ww.Accepting the loss as a normal cost of d: Accepting the loss as a normal cost is risk acceptance, where the firm keeps the risk instead of passing it to another party.

rw: Risk reduction means taking steps, such as safety training, locks or maintenance, to lower the chance or impact of a loss while the business continues its activity.

ww.Ignoring the possibility of loss or harm: Ignoring the possibility of loss does nothing to the risk; reduction requires active steps, not neglect of potential harm.
ww.Stopping the activity so the chance of l: Stopping the activity entirely is risk avoidance, which removes the chance of loss instead of just lowering it.
ww.Buying insurance for the loss that could: Buying insurance is risk transfer, because it shifts the cost of a loss to an insurer instead of lowering its chance.

rw: Cameras and alarms lower the chance and impact of theft without stopping business, which makes this risk reduction, a safety and security step.

ww.Risk avoidance: Avoidance would mean not operating the shop or not stocking items worth stealing; installing cameras keeps the activity going while lowering theft risk.
ww.Risk acceptance: Acceptance would mean doing nothing and absorbing theft losses; the shop is spending money on cameras and alarms to prevent them.
ww.Risk transfer: Transfer would shift the loss to another party, such as an insurer; cameras and alarms prevent theft instead of moving the cost.

rw: Fire insurance shifts the financial burden of a possible warehouse fire to the insurer in exchange for premiums, which is risk transfer.

ww.Risk avoidance: Avoidance would mean not storing goods in the warehouse at all; buying insurance keeps the activity and the risk in place.
ww.Risk reduction: Reduction would involve sprinklers or alarms that lower the chance of fire; insurance does not make a fire less likely.
ww.Risk acceptance: Acceptance would mean paying for fire losses out of pocket; buying insurance does the reverse by passing the cost to an insurer.

rw: Choosing not to expand into a politically unstable country avoids the risk entirely by not doing the risky activity, which is risk avoidance.

ww.Risk reduction: Reduction would keep the expansion while adding safeguards; deciding not to enter the country removes the exposure altogether.
ww.Risk transfer: Transfer would shift the financial burden to another party like an insurer; the company is not passing the risk but skipping it.
ww.Risk acceptance: Acceptance would mean expanding anyway and bearing any losses; this company chose to stay out of the unstable market.

rw: Insurance is a contract in which an insurer pays for certain covered losses in exchange for premiums, letting a business share the financial burden of unexpected events.

ww.A tax paid on risky activities carried o: A tax is a government charge paid to the state; insurance is a private contract that pays covered losses and is not a tax.
ww.A savings plan that earns interest for t: A savings plan builds a balance that earns interest for the holder; insurance pays out only when a covered loss occurs.
ww.A loan that must be repaid with interest: A loan is borrowed money repaid with interest; insurance is not borrowed and does not require repayment when it pays a covered claim.

rw: A premium is the amount paid, often monthly or yearly, to buy an insurance policy, which is the price of transferring risk to the insurer.

ww.The amount the insurer pays after a loss: The amount the insurer pays after a loss is the claim payment or benefit, not the premium the policyholder pays for coverage.
ww.The profit that an insurer makes each ye: The insurer's profit is what remains after paying claims and costs; the premium is the price charged to the policyholder.
ww.The amount owed before coverage starts: The amount owed before coverage starts describes a deductible, which the policyholder pays toward a loss before the insurer pays.

rw: A deductible is the amount the policyholder pays out of pocket before insurance pays, and a higher deductible usually means a lower premium.

ww.A refund given for no claims made during: A refund for no claims is a no-claims bonus or dividend; a deductible is paid by the policyholder when a covered loss happens.
ww.The most the insurer will pay for a cove: The most the insurer will pay is the policy limit, which caps coverage; a deductible is the portion the insured pays first.
ww.The monthly cost of a policy paid by the: The regular cost of a policy is the premium; a deductible is paid only when a claim occurs and is separate from premiums.

rw: The insurer pays the loss minus the deductible: $4,500 - $1,000 = $3,500, while the policyholder bears the first $1,000.

ww.$1,000: $1,000 is only the deductible the policyholder pays; the insurer pays the rest of the covered loss after that amount, not the deductible itself.
ww.$5,500: $5,500 would result from adding the deductible to the loss, but a deductible reduces what the insurer pays, so subtract it.
ww.$4,500: $4,500 ignores the deductible; the insurer pays only the part of the loss above it, which is $3,500, not the full amount.

rw: Liability insurance covers harm or damage a business causes to others, such as a customer injury or property damage, and pays legal costs and settlements that could otherwise be ruinous.

ww.Coverage for employees' retirement and p: Retirement and pension plans are employee benefits; liability insurance covers harm a business causes to others instead of employee retirement.
ww.Coverage for a company's taxes owed to t: Taxes owed to the state are an obligation that insurance does not cover; liability insurance protects against claims of harm to others.
ww.Coverage for a business's own property a: Coverage for a business's own property and buildings is property insurance; liability insurance pays for harm caused to others, not own assets.

rw: Property insurance covers loss or damage to a business's own buildings, equipment and inventory from events like fire, storms or theft, so the firm can repair or replace what it lost.

ww.Coverage for harm caused to customers wh: Harm to customers is covered by liability insurance; property insurance pays for the business's own assets.
ww.Coverage for a worker's illness or time: A worker's illness or time off is handled by health or workers' compensation coverage, not property insurance.
ww.Coverage for a loan not repaid, paying t: Coverage that pays a lender when a borrower defaults is credit or loan default insurance, not property insurance.

rw: Workers' compensation insurance covers employees injured on the job, paying medical bills and lost wages, and protects employers from most lawsuits over workplace injuries.

ww.Coverage for a customer's complaints: Customer complaints are handled through service and quality processes; they are not insured under workers' compensation, which relates to employee injuries.
ww.Coverage for a supplier's late delivery: A supplier's late delivery is a contract or supply issue; workers' compensation covers employees hurt at work, not delivery problems.
ww.Coverage for a company's office building: Coverage of a company's office building is property insurance; workers' compensation focuses on employees' work injuries or illness.

rw: A hazard is a condition that may cause harm or loss, such as a wet floor, faulty wiring or a dangerous chemical, and spotting hazards is the first step in controlling risk.

ww.A plan for growth and new store sites: A plan for growth is a business strategy, not a hazard; hazards are conditions that can cause harm or loss.
ww.A rule that staff must follow always: A rule staff must follow is a policy or procedure; it helps manage risk but is not a hazard itself.
ww.A benefit that increases profits each ye: A benefit that raises profits is a positive result, while a hazard is a source of potential harm or loss.

rw: A wet floor with no sign is a hazard, a condition that may cause harm, because someone could slip and be injured, so it should be marked or cleaned up.

ww.Benefit: A benefit is a positive outcome or perk; a wet floor with no sign can cause falls, so it is not a benefit.
ww.Policy: A policy is a written rule; the wet floor is a physical condition that can cause harm, not a rule.
ww.Warranty: A warranty is a promise about a product's quality; a wet floor is a safety condition, not a product guarantee.

rw: A risk assessment identifies risks and judges how likely and how serious each is, so the business can rank them and decide which ones to control first.

ww.A forecast of next year's profits and sa: Forecasting profits and sales is a financial planning task; a risk assessment looks at threats and how likely and serious they are.
ww.A list of customers who might not pay, w: A list of customers who might not pay is a credit review, which covers one financial risk but not the broad assessment of all risks.
ww.A report on employees' attendance and si: A report on attendance and sick days is an HR record; a risk assessment evaluates possible losses and hazards to the business.

rw: A risk that is both likely and very costly deserves priority because it can do the most damage, so firms rank risks by likelihood and impact and tackle the worst first.

ww.One that has already been fixed fully: A risk already fixed fully needs no further attention, so it is not a priority for new action.
ww.One that no one has ever noticed yet: A risk no one has noticed cannot be ranked by likelihood or impact until it is identified; known high-impact risks come first.
ww.One that is unlikely and cheap to fix: An unlikely, cheap-to-fix risk has low priority, since it has low probability and small cost, so it can wait behind bigger risks.

rw: A contingency plan sets out what to do if something goes wrong, such as a fire, outage or supply failure, so the business can respond quickly and keep operating.

ww.A plan to hire more employees early next: Hiring more employees is a staffing decision for growth; a contingency plan prepares for problems and is not about future hiring.
ww.A plan to raise prices next year to cove: Raising prices to cover costs is a pricing decision; a contingency plan covers what to do when something goes wrong.
ww.A plan to open a new store in the city s: Opening a new store is an expansion strategy; a contingency plan is a backup response to emergencies and unexpected events.

rw: A backup generator is a contingency measure because it lets the restaurant keep operating if power fails, protecting food, sales and customers from the disruption.

ww.A hiring process plan: A hiring process plan covers recruitment steps; a backup generator prepares for power loss, which is a different concern.
ww.A price discount plan: A price discount plan is a promotion tactic; a generator does not change prices but protects operations during an outage.
ww.A marketing campaign: A marketing campaign promotes products to customers; a backup generator is not advertising, it keeps the kitchen running in an outage.

rw: Emergency funds cover unexpected costs, such as repairs or a revenue drop, without borrowing, which avoids interest and keeps the business stable.

ww.To pay for yearly advertising costs only: Yearly advertising is a planned budget item; emergency funds are for unplanned costs, not routine marketing expenses.
ww.To make employees spend more of their pa: Emergency funds protect the business; they are not designed to make employees spend more of their pay.
ww.To avoid ever earning profits from sales: Businesses exist to earn profit; reserves are meant to protect the business from shocks and do not mean avoiding profits.

rw: Fraud is intentional deception to gain something unfairly, such as falsifying records or stealing funds, and it is a crime that can bring fines and prison.

ww.A late payment made to a supplier by the: A late payment to a supplier is a breach of terms or poor cash management, but it is not intentional deception, so it is not fraud.
ww.An honest mistake in a calculation that: An honest mistake that is corrected lacks intent to deceive, so it is an error, not fraud.
ww.A legal tax deduction taken by a busines: A legal tax deduction is allowed under tax law and is not deceptive, so it is not fraud.

rw: Separating duties means no one person handles cash from start to finish, so another employee checks the work and theft becomes harder to hide and easier to catch.

ww.Keeping cash in an unlocked drawer that: An unlocked drawer anyone can open invites theft and makes it hard to trace missing cash, so it increases risk instead of reducing it.
ww.Letting one person handle all of the cas: Letting one person handle all cash with no review removes checks and makes theft easy to hide, which raises the risk of loss.
ww.Skipping end-of-day cash counts and bank: Skipping cash counts and deposits leaves cash unprotected and unverified, so theft or errors could go unnoticed for days.

rw: Cybersecurity risk is the chance of loss from attacks on computer systems and data, such as hacking, malware or data breaches, which can cost money and trust.

ww.The chance of prices falling in the mark: Prices falling in the market is market or economic risk; cybersecurity risk relates to computer systems and data.
ww.The chance of a product being returned a: Product returns after use are a quality or customer service issue, not a risk tied to computer systems or data.
ww.The chance of staff arriving late for wo: Staff arriving late is an HR attendance matter; cybersecurity risk deals with threats to computers, networks and information.

rw: Training employees to spot and report suspicious emails builds awareness, which is the best defense against phishing because attackers rely on someone being tricked into clicking.

ww.Sharing passwords by email with other st: Sharing passwords by email exposes accounts to attackers and makes phishing more effective, so it raises the risk instead of reducing it.
ww.Turning off all security updates on staf: Turning off security updates leaves known weaknesses open to attackers, which makes phishing and malware attacks more likely to succeed.
ww.Encouraging staff to click every link th: Clicking every link is exactly how phishing works, since attackers use fake links to steal passwords or install malware, so this raises risk.

rw: Financial risk is the chance a business will lose money or be unable to pay its debts, often because of heavy borrowing, falling sales or unexpected costs.

ww.The chance that a store will be remodele: Remodeling a store is a property or planning decision, not a financial risk about losing money or paying debts.
ww.The chance that products will be stolen: Stolen products from a stockroom are a theft or security risk, though the loss has some financial effect, it is not defined as financial risk.
ww.The chance that employees will resign fr: Employees resigning is a staffing or human resources risk, not a financial risk about losing money or paying debts.

rw: Heavy borrowing with falling sales makes it harder to pay interest and repay loans, so financial risk, the chance of losing money or defaulting, rises.

ww.Safety risk: Safety risk concerns physical harm to people; borrowing and falling sales affect the firm's finances, not workplace safety.
ww.Security risk: Security risk concerns theft or attacks on assets and data; heavy debt and lower sales are not security problems.
ww.Legal risk: Legal risk comes from lawsuits or breaking laws; debt and falling sales are money matters, not a legal exposure.

rw: A safety data sheet explains a chemical's hazards, safe handling, storage, first aid and emergency steps, and OSHA requires employers to make SDSs available to workers.

ww.A sheet that lists employees' pay and ta: A list of pay and tax withholding is a payroll record; a safety data sheet covers chemical hazards and handling.
ww.A sheet that shows product prices for al: A sheet showing product prices is a price list; an SDS gives safety information about hazardous chemicals, not prices.
ww.A sheet that records sales made by the s: A record of daily sales is a sales report; an SDS describes chemical hazards and safe use.

rw: The SDS lists the chemical's hazards, protective equipment and safe handling, so reading it and following the instructions comes first before using an unfamiliar chemical.

ww.Mix it with other cleaners to test how w: Mixing cleaners can create toxic gases or violent reactions, so testing them together is dangerous and never the first step.
ww.Ask a customer in the store what to do a: A customer has no training or responsibility for workplace chemicals, so asking one is unreliable and could lead to injury.
ww.Use it without looking at any instructio: Using an unknown chemical without instructions risks burns, fumes or fire, and it violates workplace safety rules.

rw: OSHA, the Occupational Safety and Health Administration, sets and enforces workplace safety and health standards, inspects workplaces and can fine employers who fail to protect workers.

ww.Collects income taxes from employers for: Collecting income taxes from employers is done by tax agencies like the IRS, not by OSHA, which handles workplace safety.
ww.Licenses all new businesses in a state o: Business licensing is handled by state or local agencies, not OSHA, whose focus is safety and health at work.
ww.Sets prices for goods sold in stores acr: Prices of goods are set by businesses in the market; OSHA does not regulate prices but deals with workplace safety.

rw: Compliance means following the laws, rules and standards that apply to the business, such as safety, labor, tax and privacy requirements, which avoids fines, lawsuits and lost trust.

ww.Advertising on as many online platforms: Advertising on many platforms is a marketing choice and does not mean a business is following laws or rules.
ww.Hiring as many employees as the budget w: Hiring many employees is a staffing decision; compliance is about meeting legal and regulatory requirements, not headcount.
ww.Choosing the lowest prices to attract mo: Choosing low prices is a pricing strategy; compliance concerns obeying legal and regulatory requirements, not pricing choices.

rw: A regulation is a rule made by a government agency that businesses must follow, and it carries the force of law, with penalties such as fines for violations.

ww.A discount offered to businesses that pa: A discount for early taxpayers is a tax incentive, not a regulation, which is a binding rule rather than a reward.
ww.A suggestion that businesses may ignore: Regulations are mandatory; a suggestion businesses may ignore would be a guideline or recommendation, not a binding rule.
ww.A contract between two private companies: A contract between two private companies is a private agreement, not a government rule, so it is not a regulation.

rw: A compliance officer makes sure the company follows laws, regulations and internal policies by monitoring, training staff and investigating issues, which reduces legal and financial risk.

ww.To design advertisements for the company: Designing advertisements is a marketing role; a compliance officer checks that the company follows laws and policies.
ww.To repair equipment used in the company': Repairing equipment is a maintenance job; compliance officers focus on rules and legal requirements, not machinery.
ww.To set the prices that customers pay for: Pricing is a management and marketing decision, while a compliance officer ensures legal and policy adherence.

rw: A code of conduct is a written set of rules for ethical and professional behavior, telling employees what is expected on honesty, conflicts of interest, respect and legal compliance.

ww.A list of products offered by the compan: A list of products offered is a catalog; a code of conduct describes expected behavior, not what the company sells.
ww.A secret list of passwords used by the m: Passwords are confidential security credentials; a code of conduct is a shared document of behavior standards, not a secret list.
ww.A schedule of employee shifts for the wh: A schedule of shifts is a staffing plan; a code of conduct sets behavior expectations, not working hours.

rw: An expensive gift from a supplier seeking a contract may influence the employee's decision, creating a conflict of interest or looking like a bribe, which breaks most company policies and some laws.

ww.A normal service practice accepted in mo: Accepting costly gifts from someone seeking a contract is not normal practice; most firms have gift policies to prevent bias and bribery.
ww.A requirement of tax law for all employe: Tax law does not require employees to take supplier gifts; gifts are a conduct issue and may even need to be reported.
ww.A way to lower company costs and raise y: A gift does not lower company costs, and it can lead to unfair contracts and legal trouble that hurt profits.

rw: Whistleblowing is reporting illegal or unethical activity inside an organization to those who can act, and many laws protect whistleblowers from retaliation.

ww.Quitting a job without notice to start w: Quitting without notice to take another job is just resigning abruptly; it is not reporting wrongdoing.
ww.Asking a manager for a raise in pay afte: Asking for a raise is a pay negotiation, unrelated to reporting illegal or unethical conduct.
ww.Spreading false rumors about a coworker: Spreading false rumors is harmful gossip or defamation, while whistleblowing reports real wrongdoing to the proper people.

rw: OSHA is the federal agency that sets and enforces workplace safety and health standards, inspecting workplaces and fining employers that put workers at risk.

ww.An agency that sets interest rates for t: Setting interest rates is done by a central bank, such as the Federal Reserve, not OSHA, which is a workplace safety agency.
ww.An agency that collects federal income t: Collecting federal income taxes is the IRS's job, not OSHA's, which regulates safety in workplaces.
ww.An agency that approves new drugs for sa: Approving new drugs is the job of the Food and Drug Administration, not OSHA, which focuses on workplace safety.

rw: OSHA enforces workplace safety standards, including machine guarding, so it may investigate an injury caused by removed safety guards and can issue citations and fines.

ww.FCC: The FCC regulates radio, television and communications, not workplace safety injuries, so it would not investigate a removed machine guard.
ww.SEC: The SEC regulates securities markets and public company disclosures, not workplace safety, so it would not investigate this injury.
ww.Fed: The Fed is the central bank that handles monetary policy and banking supervision, not workplace injuries.

rw: The EEOC enforces federal laws against workplace discrimination based on race, sex, religion, age, disability and other protected traits, and it investigates complaints and can sue employers.

ww.Laws that set the minimum prices of good: Setting minimum prices of goods is not an EEOC role; prices are set by markets and, in some cases, other agencies.
ww.Laws that regulate all stock trading: Stock trading is regulated by the SEC, not the EEOC, which deals with employment discrimination.
ww.Laws that control imports and exports: Imports and exports are controlled by customs and trade agencies, not by the EEOC.

rw: Refusing to hire a qualified applicant because of religion is illegal discrimination under Title VII of the Civil Rights Act, and the employer could face an EEOC complaint and lawsuits.

ww.A required hiring practice: No law requires hiring decisions based on religion; employers must judge applicants on qualifications, not protected traits.
ww.A legal hiring preference: Religion is a protected characteristic, so preferring or rejecting applicants for it is not a legal hiring preference.
ww.A tax compliance step: Hiring decisions are not tax compliance steps; this is a discrimination issue, not something tax rules require.

rw: The FLSA sets federal minimum wage, overtime pay rules and child labor limits, protecting workers by requiring pay for covered hours and limiting hazardous work by minors.

ww.Rules for food labeling on all packages: Food labeling is regulated by the FDA and related agencies, not by the FLSA, which covers pay and labor rules.
ww.Rules for advertising claims in the news: Advertising claims are overseen by the FTC; the FLSA deals with wages, hours and child labor.
ww.Rules for stock market trading and broke: Stock market trading and broker reports fall under securities law enforced by the SEC, not the Fair Labor Standards Act.

rw: First 40 hours: 40 x $14 = $560. Overtime rate is $14 x 1.5 = $21, so 4 x $21 = $84. Total is $560 + $84 = $644.

ww.$924: $924 would come from paying all 44 hours at overtime rate (44 x $21); only the 4 hours beyond 40 earn overtime pay.
ww.$616: $616 is 44 x $14 at straight time, which ignores the extra half-time premium owed for the 4 overtime hours.
ww.$560: $560 covers only the first 40 hours at $14, leaving out the 4 overtime hours that also earn pay at $21 each.

rw: Records prove the company followed required rules, such as tax, safety and employment laws, which helps pass audits, defend against claims and show good faith to regulators.

ww.To increase the number of forms employee: Record keeping aims to document compliance, not to create more paperwork for employees to fill out.
ww.To raise product prices for customers ea: Records do not set prices; their purpose is to document actions, not to raise what customers pay.
ww.To hide mistakes from regulators and fro: Hiding mistakes from regulators would be unethical and illegal; proper records are meant to be accurate and available for review.

rw: The best response is to complete the training, fix the records and set up a tracking system, which corrects the gap and prevents it from happening again.

ww.Ignore the finding until the next audit: Ignoring a finding leaves the violation in place, risks fines and injuries, and will likely be flagged again at the next audit.
ww.Blame the auditor for the finding and ar: Blaming the auditor does not fix missing records and wastes time; audit findings are meant to help improve compliance.
ww.Destroy the audit report so no one sees: Destroying an audit report is illegal obstruction and hides problems instead of solving them, which can lead to serious penalties.

rw: A license is official permission from a government or authority to operate a business or practice a profession, such as a liquor license or a medical license, and operating without one can bring penalties.

ww.A list of company rules that all staff m: A list of company rules is a policy or code of conduct; a license is permission granted by an authority.
ww.A discount for buying in bulk, given to: A bulk discount is a pricing incentive for large orders, not an official permission to operate.
ww.A report of annual profits that a firm s: A report of annual profits is a financial statement; a license is a government grant of permission.

rw: Operating without a required health permit is illegal, so authorities can issue fines, order the restaurant closed and require it to obtain the permit before reopening.

ww.Lower taxes for the whole year ahead: Lower taxes are not a result of skipping a permit; opening without one is a violation that leads to penalties, not savings.
ww.Faster deliveries from suppliers: Supplier delivery speed is unrelated to permits; breaking health rules does not speed up deliveries.
ww.A reward from the health department: The health department enforces rules and would not reward a violation; it is more likely to punish an unpermitted restaurant.

rw: Data privacy compliance means following laws that protect personal information, such as rules on collecting, storing, sharing and deleting data, so customers' details stay safe and the firm avoids fines.

ww.Storing data on unlocked shared public c: Storing data on unlocked public computers leaves it exposed and violates privacy duties, so it is the opposite of compliance.
ww.Selling personal data without telling cu: Selling personal data without telling customers violates privacy laws that require notice and often consent, so it breaks compliance.
ww.Sharing customer data with anyone who as: Sharing customer data with anyone who asks breaches privacy duties and risks identity theft, so it is a violation, not compliance.

rw: The company should check applicable privacy laws and its retention policy, which say what data may be kept, for how long and when it must be deleted.

ww.Only the color of the email design and f: The color and font of an email design have no bearing on how long data must be kept; legal and policy rules decide retention.
ww.Only the number of customers on the emai: The size of the list does not determine retention; laws and policies decide how long personal data may or must be kept.
ww.Nothing, because emails can be kept fore: Personal data cannot be kept forever by anyone, since privacy laws often limit retention and require deletion when it is no longer needed.

rw: An internal control is a procedure, such as approvals, reconciliations or separation of duties, that protects assets, prevents fraud and ensures accurate records.

ww.A schedule of employee shifts for the ne: A schedule of shifts is a staffing plan, not a procedure that safeguards assets or the accuracy of records.
ww.A rule that sets the price of a product,: Setting a product's price is a pricing decision; internal controls are procedures that protect the business, not price rules.
ww.A tool for advertising to customers on t: Advertising on radio and in print is a promotion activity, while internal controls protect assets and records.

rw: Separating the duties of approving and paying invoices means one person cannot create and pay a fake invoice alone, which reduces the risk of fraud and errors.

ww.It is required for every business bank a: No rule requires this for every bank account; the practice is a recommended internal control, not a universal requirement.
ww.It lowers the cost of the invoices a fir: Separation of duties does not lower invoice costs; its goal is control and accuracy, not cost reduction.
ww.It makes payments take longer to complet: The aim is protection against fraud, not slower payments; good controls can be built without much delay.

rw: The Sarbanes-Oxley Act, passed in 2002 after scandals like Enron, requires accurate and honest financial reporting by public companies and holds executives accountable with internal controls and audits.

ww.Rules for food safety in restaurants and: Food safety rules come from agencies like the FDA and local health departments, not from the Sarbanes-Oxley Act.
ww.Setting the minimum wage for workers in: The minimum wage is set by the Fair Labor Standards Act and state laws, not by Sarbanes-Oxley.
ww.Limits on imports from other countries a: Import limits and port duties are trade and customs matters, not covered by Sarbanes-Oxley.

rw: A conflict of interest is a situation where personal interests could affect job decisions, such as hiring a relative, so it should be disclosed and handled to keep decisions fair.

ww.A disagreement over office furniture, su: A disagreement over furniture is an ordinary workplace dispute; a conflict of interest involves personal interests affecting work decisions.
ww.A rivalry between two stores in the same: Rivalry between competing stores is normal competition, not a conflict of interest, which concerns one person's divided loyalties.
ww.A debate about a company's slogan and it: A debate over a slogan is a creative disagreement, not a situation where personal interests could affect job decisions.

rw: The manager should disclose the relationship and step away from the decision so others can judge the bids fairly, which protects the company and the manager.

ww.Ask the sibling to hide the ownership of: Asking a sibling to hide ownership adds deception to the conflict and worsens the violation instead of fixing it.
ww.Keep it secret to avoid questions from t: Keeping the relationship secret hides the conflict of interest and could look like favoritism or fraud if discovered.
ww.Award it anyway as the price was fair an: A fair price does not remove the conflict; the issue is the undisclosed relationship, not the cost, and secrecy still breaks policy.

rw: An ethics hotline is a confidential way for employees to report concerns about misconduct, fraud or safety, often anonymously, so problems surface without fear of retaliation.

ww.A number that customers call to place or: A number for customers to place orders is a sales line, not an ethics hotline, which handles reports of misconduct.
ww.A number used to reset passwords for sta: Password resets are an IT help desk function, not an ethics hotline, which is meant for reporting concerns.
ww.A number used to schedule deliveries to: A line to schedule deliveries is a logistics service, not an ethics hotline for reporting wrongdoing.

rw: A policy is a formal statement of the rules a company expects people to follow, guiding decisions and behavior so that everyone acts consistently and legally.

ww.A list of the goods in storage at the ma: A list of goods in storage is an inventory record; a policy is a statement of rules for people to follow.
ww.A short-term plan for one project, endin: A short-term plan for one project is a project plan, not a policy, which is an ongoing rule guiding behavior.
ww.A message sent to customers and the pres: A message about a new product is a press release or announcement, not a policy that sets rules for staff.

rw: When policies are communicated and enforced consistently, all employees understand the rules and are treated fairly, which reduces disputes, protects the company legally and builds trust.

ww.So that employees do not ask any questio: Policies should invite understanding, not prevent questions; employees need to ask questions to follow rules correctly.
ww.So that only managers know the rules of: Policies are meant for everyone to follow; keeping them known to managers alone would make compliance impossible.
ww.So that rules can be ignored when it sui: Ignoring rules when it suits managers is unfair and creates risk of discrimination claims, which is why enforcement must be consistent.

rw: A trademark is a word, symbol or design that identifies a brand and is legally protected, so others cannot use confusingly similar marks and consumers can recognize the source.

ww.A list of a company's competitors and al: A list of competitors and their goods is market research, not a trademark, which identifies a brand and is legally protected.
ww.A tax on branded goods that a large firm: A trademark is not a tax; it is intellectual property protection, and owners register it rather than pay tax on it.
ww.A mark showing a product was inspected b: A mark showing government inspection is a certification or grade stamp, not a trademark, which identifies a brand.

rw: Using a competitor's logo without permission is likely trademark infringement, since a logo is protected brand identity and copying it can confuse customers and bring lawsuits.

ww.Immigration law: Immigration law governs entry and work status of people, not the use of a logo.
ww.Zoning law: Zoning law controls how land and buildings may be used, not whether a logo can be copied.
ww.Minimum wage law: Minimum wage law sets pay rules for workers and does not cover copying a competitor's logo.

rw: A contract is a legally enforceable agreement between parties, usually requiring an offer, acceptance and consideration, and either side can seek a remedy in court if it is broken.

ww.A message sent to a customer after a sal: A message sent after a sale is a follow-up, not a binding agreement between parties.
ww.A friendly promise with no legal weight: A friendly promise with no legal weight is a casual agreement; a contract is enforceable by law.
ww.A list of a company's products and their: A list of products and prices is a catalog or price list, not an agreement between parties.

rw: Failing to deliver goods as agreed in a signed contract is a breach of contract, and the other party may seek damages, cancel the deal or demand performance.

ww.A normal delay, no cost: A signed contract creates a duty to deliver; failing to do so is not a harmless delay without cost.
ww.A marketing success: Failing to deliver is not a marketing success; it harms the customer relationship and creates legal exposure.
ww.A tax law violation: Late delivery under a contract is a contract problem, not a tax law violation, which relates to tax duties.

rw: An environmental regulation is a rule that limits pollution and protects natural resources such as air, water and soil, and businesses that break it face fines and cleanup costs.

ww.A rule that sets the price of energy for: Energy prices are set by markets and utility regulators, not by environmental regulations, which target pollution.
ww.A rule that limits advertising on televi: Limits on advertising are consumer protection or media rules, not environmental regulations.
ww.A rule that decides employee holidays an: Employee holidays and vacation are decided by employers and labor agreements, not by environmental rules.

rw: The Environmental Protection Agency enforces laws like the Clean Water Act, so it would act when a factory releases waste into a river without a permit, seeking fines and cleanup.

ww.The Small Business Administration: The Small Business Administration supports small firms with loans and advice; it does not enforce pollution laws.
ww.The Federal Reserve Board system: The Federal Reserve oversees monetary policy and banking, so it has no role in river pollution enforcement.
ww.The Social Security Administration: The Social Security Administration runs retirement and disability benefits and does not enforce environmental rules.

rw: A project is a temporary effort with a defined beginning and end that creates a unique result, such as a product launch or a new building.

ww.A list of employees' duties and job titl: A list of duties and job titles is an organization chart or job description, not a project, which has a set start and end.
ww.A permanent department within a company,: A permanent department is an ongoing part of the firm, while a project is temporary and ends when its result is delivered.
ww.An ongoing task that is repeated every d: An ongoing task repeated daily is routine operations, not a project, which is a one-time effort with an end.

rw: Project management is planning, organizing and controlling resources such as people, time and money to complete a project on time, within budget and to the required quality.

ww.Setting the price of a product for sale: Setting product prices is a marketing and finance function, not the management of a project.
ww.Delivering goods to customers by truck,: Delivering goods by truck, rail or ship is logistics and transportation, not project management.
ww.Hiring workers for permanent positions o: Hiring for permanent positions is human resources work, whereas project management coordinates temporary work toward a goal.

rw: Project scope is the work that is included in the project and what is not, which sets clear boundaries, helps control cost and time, and prevents misunderstandings with the client.

ww.The money spent on the project and the t: Money spent and time worked describe budget and effort used; scope defines which work is included in the project.
ww.The list of everyone on the project team: The team list and roles describe project staffing, not scope, which lays out what work is and is not included.
ww.The date the project will end and be clo: The end date is part of the schedule, not the scope, which describes the work to be done.

rw: Scope creep is the gradual growth of a project's work beyond the original plan, such as a client adding features without matching changes to time or budget, which can cause delays and overruns.

ww.Quality control: Quality control checks that outputs meet standards; adding requested features partway through is a change of scope.
ww.Benchmarking: Benchmarking compares performance with the best in the industry; it has nothing to do with clients adding features.
ww.Risk transfer: Risk transfer shifts the financial burden of a risk to another party, such as through insurance, and does not describe added client requests.

rw: The best way is to evaluate each change for time, cost and risk and approve it only through a formal change process, which keeps the project controlled and the client informed.

ww.Cancel the project immediately and send: Canceling the project immediately is an extreme reaction that wastes work already done and fails the client.
ww.Accept every request without question so: Accepting every request without question causes scope creep, which pushes the project over budget and past its deadline.
ww.Ignore the client and keep working on th: Ignoring the client damages the relationship; legitimate changes can be handled through proper review instead of being dismissed.

rw: A project manager leads the team and makes sure the project meets its goals for scope, schedule, budget and quality, coordinating people and resources and communicating with stakeholders.

ww.Setting the company's long-term mission: Setting the company's long-term mission and values is the job of senior executives, not a project manager.
ww.Doing every task in the project alone, w: A project manager coordinates and leads the team; doing every task alone would be impossible and defeats the purpose of teamwork.
ww.Selling the project's results to custome: Selling a project's results is a sales role; the project manager focuses on delivering the project.

rw: A stakeholder is anyone affected by or interested in the project, such as sponsors, team members, customers and the community, so managers must keep them informed and consider their needs.

ww.Only the competitors of the company that: Competitors are outside parties that may not be affected by the project; stakeholders include many groups beyond rivals.
ww.Only the person who pays for the project: The funder is only one stakeholder; employees, customers and others affected by the project also count.
ww.Only the project manager and the people: The project manager and team are stakeholders, but so are sponsors, customers and others, so the group is much wider.

rw: A milestone is a significant point or achievement in a project schedule, such as completing a design or passing testing, and it helps managers track progress.

ww.The total cost of the project, from the: The total cost of a project is the budget; a milestone is a significant point in the schedule.
ww.A daily task for one team member, marked: A daily task for one team member is a small work item, not a significant project checkpoint like a milestone.
ww.A risk that has happened and caused a de: A risk that has happened and caused delay is an issue, not a milestone, which marks progress.

rw: A Gantt chart is a bar chart that shows project tasks over time, with each bar marking when a task starts and ends, so managers can see the schedule and overlaps.

ww.A diagram that shows who reports to whom: A diagram showing who reports to whom is an organization chart, not a Gantt chart, which displays tasks over time.
ww.A pie chart that shows the budget parts: A pie chart showing budget parts is a different kind of graph, not a Gantt chart, which tracks time.
ww.A table that lists customers' names: A table listing customer names is a customer list, not a Gantt chart, which charts tasks over a timeline.

rw: A Gantt chart shows when each task starts and ends along a timeline and how tasks overlap, which makes it the standard tool for project scheduling.

ww.A pie chart: A pie chart shows parts of a whole, such as budget shares, but not timing or overlap of tasks.
ww.A customer survey: A customer survey gathers opinions from buyers and does not show project schedules or task overlap.
ww.A balance sheet: A balance sheet reports a firm's assets, liabilities and equity at a point in time, not project tasks.

rw: The critical path is the longest sequence of dependent tasks, which determines the project's minimum length, so any delay on it delays the whole project.

ww.The list of tasks that can be skipped wi: Tasks that can be skipped without harm are not on the critical path; critical tasks cannot be skipped without affecting the project.
ww.The most expensive set of tasks, which c: The critical path is about time, not cost; the most expensive tasks may not determine the project's minimum length.
ww.The shortest route between two offices f: The shortest route between offices is a travel concept; the critical path in project management is about task sequence and time.

rw: Because the critical path sets the project's length, a three-day delay pushes the end date back three days unless the team makes up time, such as by adding resources.

ww.Nothing, because the other tasks will ca: Tasks on the critical path have no slack, so other tasks cannot automatically make up the lost time.
ww.The project budget becomes zero and the: A delay does not erase the budget or stop the work; it affects the schedule and can raise costs.
ww.The project finishes three days early, w: A delay on the critical path cannot make the project finish early; it pushes the schedule later.

rw: A project budget is the estimated money needed to complete the project, including labor, materials and other costs, and managers track spending against it.

ww.The list of tasks for the project and wh: The list of tasks and start dates is the project schedule or work plan, not the budget, which covers money.
ww.The date by which the project must end a: The date a project must end is the deadline in the schedule, not the budget.
ww.The group of people who are working on t: The people on the project team are the staff or resources, not the budget, which is about estimated costs.

rw: $30,000 of $50,000 is 60 percent spent for 50 percent of the work, so costs are ahead of progress and the project may finish over budget unless it is corrected.

ww.It will finish under budget: Spending 60 percent of the budget ($30,000 of $50,000) for only 50 percent of the work suggests costs are running ahead of progress, so finishing under budget is unlikely.
ww.It is already fully complete: With only 50 percent of the work done, the project is not complete, so this answer is wrong.
ww.It has no budget problem: Spending 60 percent of the budget for 50 percent of the work is a warning sign, so saying there is no problem ignores the data.

rw: A project risk is an uncertain event that could affect the project, positively or negatively, such as a supplier delay or a change in scope, and managers plan responses in advance.

ww.The final report of the project, due at: A final report is a project deliverable at the end; a risk is an uncertain event that might happen.
ww.The name of the project team chosen by i: The name of a project team is a label, not an uncertain event that could affect the project.
ww.A task that is already finished and sign: A finished and signed-off task is a completed item, not an uncertain event, which is what a risk is.

rw: Planning ahead, such as lining up a backup supplier, is a risk response that keeps the project on schedule if the key supplier is late.

ww.Hope the supplier is on time and make no: Hoping the supplier is on time with no plan leaves the project exposed if the delay happens, so it is not good risk management.
ww.Blame the supplier before any delay happ: Blaming the supplier before any delay happens fixes nothing and harms the relationship, while the risk remains unmanaged.
ww.Remove the task from the plan for the pr: Removing the task from the plan does not remove the need for the supplier's work and would leave the project incomplete.
